stories.headline: G7 moves to release oil and diesel reserves as attacks disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz

sources.body:
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.

It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.

The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.

Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports , there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.

The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.

Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.

On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."

His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."

"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said.

"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."

Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
sources.headline: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat

sources.body:
Global energy prices have been soaring due to the US and Israel’s war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine.

The Group of Seven countries has agreed to release 100 billion barrels of crude oil and diesel from emergency reserves over several months in an effort to reduce soaring energy prices after pressure from US President Donald Trump.

The US and Israel’s war on Iran, as well as Russia’s war on Ukraine, have triggered a spike in global oil and diesel prices.

Oil prices ‌jumped on Thursday and settled up more than $4 a barrel. Global diesel prices also hit a record high last Friday with the average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) of diesel at $6.50, up from $5.61 a month earlier, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

In a statement on Thursday, G7, which includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented, said there will also be a “substantial diesel release within the first 20 days” and discussions over “additional diesel releases as necessary” will be held in the coming days.

Will the G7’s energy release stabilise the global energy market?

After a video conference of G7 leaders chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday, the group said in a joint statement: “Taking into account commitments that have already been fulfilled, we will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels.”

Earlier this week, the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Executive Director Fatih Birol said that members had released about two-thirds of the 400-million-barrel agreement.

The G7 energy release will begin immediately and last for four months and will include a substantial diesel release for 20 days. It is not clear how many oil and diesel stocks each member of the group will release.

“We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary,” the statement said.

“We will coordinate maintenance schedules across G7 refineries to prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible,” it added.

The G7 also urged member countries to refrain from imposing export restrictions on energy products among themselves.

Earlier this week, the Trump administration had threatened to impose a ban on US diesel exports and also pressured Europe to release its emergency diesel stocks to help ease soaring diesel prices.

Global energy prices have been soaring due to the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has disrupted energy exports from the Gulf. Meanwhile, the Ukraine attacks on Russian energy installations have also disrupted global energy supplies.

Former head of the International Energy Agency’s Oil Industry and Markets Division Neil Atkinson told Al Jazeera that there are three key factors contributing to the decline in global diesel supply.

First, “there isn’t diesel coming out of the Middle East to Europe, and Europe took quite a lot of diesel from Saudi Arabia and from Kuwait.”
sources.headline: G7 nations to release oil and diesel stocks, will it bring down the prices?

stories.headline: Brazil prepares for a closely contested presidential election between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro

sources.body: President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will stand for re-election in Brazil on Sunday. At 80, the former steelworker hopes to capitalise on his popularity and economic successes to win a fourth term in office but is neck-and-neck in the polls with far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro.
sources.headline: Brazil’s Lula gears up for ‘last dance’ with run for fourth presidential term

sources.body:
Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup

‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election

S hortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.

“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.

Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.

On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.

Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.

Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro , 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.

“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum , is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.

“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.

Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs ” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land .

While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.

Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth , but it is currently at a low point , with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.
sources.headline: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc

sources.body:
For a third election in a row, a member of the Bolsonaro family is the leading right-wing contender for Brazil's presidency.

Sao Paulo, Brazil – Much has changed since the far-right army captain Jair Bolsonaro won Brazil's presidency in 2018.

Last year, the former president was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn his 2022 election defeat. In 2023, he was barred from holding public office for eight years after a court determined he abused his political office.

He is currently banned from using social media. His last post was published in July 2025.

And yet, Bolsonaro has forged a powerful political dynasty that is on the verge of returning to power in Brazil's October presidential election.

His eldest son, 45-year-old Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, is in a statistical tie with the race's incumbent, left-leaning President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

A September 24 poll released by the public opinion firm Datafolha showed Lula with a slim lead in a simulated run-off, earning 47 percent support to Flavio's 45 percent, well within the margin of error.

Other pollsters predict an even narrower gap between the two frontrunners.

Like his father, Flavio has faced investigation and scandal. But experts say the Bolsonaro family has endured as a political force in part by harnessing decades of frustration with Lula's Workers' Party (PT).

That resentment, in turn, has transformed into a potent election-season brand.

“There is a hyperfocus on Lula and the PT, who for over two decades have been branded by many conservatives as the ones solely responsible for rampant corruption,” said political scientist Paulo Roberto Souza of the Democracy in Check Institute, an independent research nonprofit.

Analysts told Al Jazeera that the Bolsonaro family's electoral strength does not come from a base of hardcore supporters.

Bolsonaristas, after all, are only estimated to comprise between 15 and 25 percent of Brazil's electorate. Instead, experts credit "antipetismo" — a trend of hostility against Lula's PT movement — with fuelling the Bolsonaro family's rise to political power.

The PT has won all but one of the last six presidential elections in Brazil. The only exception has been Jair Bolsonaro himself, with his 2018 win.

Jair Bolsonaro did not invent "antipetismo", according to Mario Sergio Lima, a Brazil analyst at Medley Advisors, a political advisory firm.

But his arrival as a presidential frontrunner in 2018 gave the movement a political identity, Lima said. The elder Bolsonaro was able to “condense anti-PT sentiment into his own persona”.

Lima predicted Flavio would likewise benefit from the wave of "antipetismo" when he competes against Lula in the October 4 general election.

“It is easy for anyone who is already against the PT to vote for Flavio or anyone who carries the Bolsonaro name, because Jair managed to personify a feeling that already existed in Brazilian society,” Lima explained.

Formerly a long-serving member of Brazil's Chamber of Deputies, Jair Bolsonaro has become the fulcrum for a political movement based around his own nuclear family.
sources.headline: A political dynasty? Why the Bolsonaro family dominates Brazil’s right wing

stories.headline: Russia strikes another major bridge across Kyiv’s Dnipro River

sources.body:
A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko has said, as Russia ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital.

The attack on Saturday morning damaged the road surface and trolleybus overhead wires on the Northern (Pivnichnyi) Bridge, Klitschko said, causing traffic to be blocked.

The strike comes after another key bridge in the city, Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge, was targeted multiple times by Russian drones on Thursday and Friday, with Klitschko earlier warning that such attacks were "tearing Kyiv apart" .

The Northern and Southern bridges link the eastern and western parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday, signalling a new stage in Moscow's strategy.

Attacks on the Southern Bridge have caused major travel disruption since Thursday, with metro and car travel across it suspended.

Many of the city's residents - which number about three million - rely on the metro to travel across the city.

Writing on Telegram on Saturday, Klitschko said: "Hitting the North Bridge. Emergency services are on their way."

"Traffic on the bridge from the left to the right bank is currently blocked," he added.

Russia's defence ministry said it had hit the bridge, saying it was used for military troop transfers and logistics.

It also said it targeted a logistics centre in the city. Klitschko did not mention this.

Earlier attacks on the Southern Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday, prompting Klitschko to warn afterwards that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.

After the Southern Bridge was attacked, passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided that there were "no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.

In an interview with the Financial Times, he said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings."

He added: "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
sources.headline: Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says

sources.body: Kyiv's Northern Bridge across the Dnipro river was hit by a Russian air attack, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Saturday, amid an escalation in strikes ​on ‌infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital. The attack comes a day after the city's Southern Bridge was hit by several strikes that officials said were "tearing Kyiv apart".
sources.headline: Russia strikes another major bridge across Kyiv's Dnipro river

sources.body:
Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge

V aleriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.

“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.

A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”

Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.

He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.

On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.

Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.

For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.

“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko , said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”

This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.

“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.

Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.

The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.
sources.headline: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks

stories.headline: UAE says Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with a crash axe in alleged terrorist act

sources.body:
The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.

The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.

Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.

Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.

The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.

The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.

While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.

He completed a three-year distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"

The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."

He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".

The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.

Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.

The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.

"I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.

About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply.

The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking.

In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong.

Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down."
sources.headline: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says

sources.body:
Attorney general says ‘terrorist attack’ was attempted by suspect who is said to have been barred from flying by Oman because of extremist views

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used a crash axe to attempt to carry out a “terrorist attack” during the flight, the United ⁠Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to a state news agency.

The UAE statement cited the prosecutor general as saying the co-pilot also tried to take control of the plane during Wednesday’s attack on the Israel-bound flight. Passengers and crew intervened to subdue the co-pilot and stabilise the plane. Officials said the co-pilot’s actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board by sending it into a sharp plunge.

A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for ⁠use during emergencies.

The co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a person familiar with the matter said. He was then hired by the United Arab Emirates-based airline flydubai, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. Oman’s barring of him was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators . Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots out of its airspace who come from nations with which it does not maintain diplomatic relations. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.

The official confirmed that the co-pilot worked with Oman’s national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views. He was later moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, the official said.

Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other western governments, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.

UAE senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash on Friday called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act”. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.

Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation” but provided no evidence.

The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed loud noises to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the plane. It made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Both the captain and co-pilot were taken to the UAE as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.
sources.headline: Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE

sources.body:
Probe ⁠under way to ​determine ‘all the ⁠circumstances’, including motive, UAE’s prosecutor general says.

The prosecutor general of the United Arab Emirates has said a Flydubai co-pilot “attempted to carry out a terrorist act” during a flight earlier this week, using a crash axe against the pilot inside the cockpit.

State news agency WAM quoted Hamad Saif al-Shamsi as saying on Saturday that the attacker of Wednesday’s flight FZ1073 tried to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls.

He said the investigation is under way “to uncover all the circumstances of the incident, its motives, and related connections, in addition to completing technical examinations and examining physical and digital evidence”.

The final results will be announced as soon as the necessary procedures are completed, al-Shamsi said.

A crash axe is a tool kept in a cockpit to help pilots cut through the plane in emergencies.

The plane carrying 174 passengers was on its way from the UAE’s Dubai to Israel’s Tel Aviv on Wednesday when a co-pilot wounded Indian pilot Smit Machchhar who opened the cockpit to seek help.

The attacker was not officially identified, but media reports quoting unnamed sources claimed he was Omani national Hamam al-Hammami .

The aircraft briefly plunged about 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control by a second paid of new pilots after passengers and crew subdued the attacker.

The flight was diverted and forced to make an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

The co-pilot was arrested by Saudi authorities and handed over to the UAE as it leads the probe.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that ⁠Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone’s direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”.

Flydubai halted all flights its Israel route after the incident and Israel’s El Al cancelled its scheduled flights, stranding some Israelis in the UAE.

At 22:00 GMT on Friday, the first repatriation flight, operated by Israeli carrier Arkia, arrived at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport from Dubai.
sources.headline: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with crash axe in ‘terrorist act’: UAE

stories.headline: North Korea launches ballistic missile amid renewed tensions with South Korea

sources.body: North Korea launched a ballistic missile Saturday morning from the Wonsan area on its east coast into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea's military. The launch comes amid renewed tensions between Pyongyang and Seoul, with the latter demanding an apology for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarized Zone last month.
sources.headline: North Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts

sources.body:
Pyongyang fires towards sea a day after Kim Jong-un sister denounces South Korea for claiming North’s mines wounded South’s soldiers in DMZ

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, ⁠a day ​after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.

The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.

Japan’s ⁠coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been ​a ballistic missile and appeared to have come ‌down, warning ships to take ‌precautions.

South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.

Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, ​issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.

Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.

South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured ⁠three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches ​across the Korean peninsula.

The missile ​test might be an attempt ​by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, ​said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president ‌at the Sejong ​Institute in Seoul, ​a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.

North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.

North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.
sources.headline: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers

sources.body:
A ballistic missile fired from the North Korean port city of Wonsan flies more than 700km, South Korea’s military says.

South Korea’s military says North Korea has fired at least one ballistic missile towards the sea off its east coast.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Saturday morning that its northern neighbour fired a ballistic missile from the port city of Wonsan on the eastern shore of the Korean Peninsula and that it flew more than 700 kilometres (435 miles).

Seoul’s presidential national security office convened an emergency meeting to assess the situation after the launch, the president’s office said in a statement.

The South Korean military raised an alert for further launches and said it would share intelligence with the US and Japan.

Japan issued an emergency alert on Saturday, saying: “North Korea has launched a suspected ballistic missile.”

The US Pacific Command said it was aware of the launch, adding that it was consulting closely with US allies and partners.

“Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies,” it said in a social media post.

The launch came a day after Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologise over landmine blasts that South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command said were caused by North Korean mines planted south of the Military Demarcation Line.

The blasts seriously injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide (2.5-mile) border zone that stretches across the Korean Peninsula.

South Korea has also called on the North to halt recent efforts to fortify its border, including the installation of mines and anti-tank barriers.

Kim Yo Jong dismissed Seoul’s demands as “utterly pathetic”, saying the North intends to permanently cut ties with the South.

Saturday’s launch was the latest in a series of North Korean military displays in recent weeks, including tests of a purported hypersonic missile system, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship.
sources.headline: North Korea fires ballistic missile towards the sea, South Korea says

stories.headline: Tigray rebels reportedly abandon Mekelle as Ethiopian federal forces advance

sources.body: Rebels from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) in Ethiopia were abandoning their regional capital of Mekkele in the north of the country on Saturday, according to local reports. The TPLF has been fighting against federal forces and pro-government militias since September 23 and launching attacks into neighbouring states, raising fears of an all-out civil war similar to that of 2020-2022.
sources.headline: Ethiopia's Tigray rebels abandon regional capital of Mekelle as pro-government forces advance

sources.body: First, Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed ties and now with tensions spreading across the region, the African Union is urging all sides to show restraint. Meanwhile, Ethiopia's army is advancing toward the Tigrayan capital as fighting intensifies and new explosions rock Addis Ababa. Then, from boardrooms to cocoa fields, a growing number of urban Ivorians are turning to agriculture. On weekends, civil servants, entrepreneurs and traders leave Abidjan behind to tend farms in the countryside, seeking extra income. But running a plantation from afar comes with challenges. And, Senegal is counting down to a historic moment. In a few weeks, Dakar will host the 2026 Youth Olympic Games: the first Olympic event ever staged in Africa. But the stakes go far beyond sport. We speak to Senegal’s Minister of Sports, Djirèye Clotilde Coly.
sources.headline: Ethiopian army pushes back Tigrayan rebels

stories.headline: WHO warns delayed aid access could have devastating consequences in Gaza

sources.body:
The WHO’s representative in Palestine calls on Israeli authorities to “release the pressure on medical supplies”.

Repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies from Israel into Gaza risk having “devastating consequences” for Palestinians who urgently need them, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

Approved aid can enter Gaza only through Kerem Shalom, at the southern tip of the territory, while Rafah, also in the south, is open only for limited movement of people, including patients needing medical treatment abroad, the WHO said on Friday.

“A truck full of non-priority supplies or the right supplies arriving too late , doesn’t save lives. That’s the question that actually matters,” Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, the WHO’s representative in Palestine, said.

Van De Weerdt called on Israeli authorities to “release the pressure on medical supplies”, saying essential medicines “should not be considered as dual use, as they are globally accepted standards on medical items anybody needs anywhere to run a hospital or a clinic”.

She added that one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices had been rejected four times over the past six months.

“Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again,” she said, noting that medicines “by contrast, move relatively well”, with almost 87 percent approved and just over 1 percent rejected.

“Our ask is simple and has not changed: we need the unimpeded and predictable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza at scale. We also need a multi-crossing model so that aid isn’t forced to trickle down through a limited number of crossings,” Van De Weerdt said.

Four other main entry points into Gaza – Kissufim, Gate 96, Erez and Erez West – remain closed and under total Israeli control.

She praised the “extraordinary health workers” still risking their lives in Gaza, who she said were not receiving enough supplies to give patients the care they needed.

“As winter begins, this urgency to get supplies into Gaza only deepens,” Van De Weerdt said. “Almost two million people are in need of shelter to protect against the cold and the risk of flooding, exposing people to serious health and safety risks, let alone their dignity.”

She said residents faced a heightened risk of preventable disease outbreaks linked to the lack of safe shelter and clean water, and a high number of rats whose bites transmit infection, a threat made harder to track by the destruction of public health laboratories.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned on Thursday of serious public health risks from the accumulation of solid waste in Gaza City, where sanitation gains remain fragile because of a lack of reliable access to heavy machinery, engine oil, spare parts and fuel funding.

Almost 12 months into a fragile “ceasefire” between Hamas and Israel, marked by continuing Israeli air attacks and other military activity, Gaza’s humanitarian situation remains “overwhelming”, according to OCHA.
sources.headline: WHO warns of ‘devastating consequences’ due to delayed aid entry into Gaza

No warning given before Israeli deadly strike hit Remal area, one of Gaza City’s most densely populated neighbourhoods.

Israeli air attack on residential apartment in Gaza kills 5 Palestinians

An Israeli air attack on a residential apartment in western Gaza City has killed at least five people and severely wounded several others, according to medical staff at al-Shifa Hospital.

The strike hit the al-Asala building in the Remal neighbourhood early on Saturday without prior warning, according to Al Jazeera’s Hani al-Shaer, reporting from Khan Younis.

Remal is one of Gaza City’s most crowded residential areas, home to thousands of displaced people sheltering in makeshift camps across the neighbourhood.

Al-Shaer said the attack came in the middle of the night, when residents were asleep.

“We heard fighter jets getting louder, then three strikes followed, hitting the apartment and killing those inside,” he said.

The strike penetrated the targeted apartment and tore through the floors below, causing further destruction throughout the multistorey building.

Reporting from Gaza City later on Saturday, Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary described yet “another terrifying night”.

“Around 2am [on Saturday, 11:00 GMT on Friday], two huge explosions shook the al-Haid roundabout. We later learned that the Israeli army targeted a building with two explosive drones, killing at least three women, a child and a young man.”

Fires burned for at least an hour before Palestinian Civil Defence crews managed to put them out. Al-Shaer described the scene as “horrific”, while Khoudary said “the whole neighbourhood was shaken”, as people were buried under the rubble as they slept.

Civil defence crews were still searching the site for missing people and bodies, al-Shaer said, as Israeli drones continued flying over the area and fighter jets were heard flying low across the Strip.

“This is not the first ceasefire violation, or the first attack, in the past 24 hours,” Khoudary noted, as an Israeli drone strike killed a Palestinian man and wounded several others in southern Gaza on Thursday.

“According to doctors, it is very, very hard to save the lives of those who are injured, because Israel continues to restrict medical supplies and instruments,” Khoudary said. “A lot of people are queueing to leave the Gaza Strip through the Rafah crossing.”

Bordering Egypt in the south of Gaza, the Rafah crossing is only opened by Israeli forces for limited movements of people, especially patients needing medical treatment abroad, the World Health Organization (WHO) said .

Repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies from Israel into Gaza are having “devastating consequences” for Palestinians who urgently need them, the WHO said on Saturday.

Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and more than 175,000 have been injured, according to the enclave’s Health Ministry. The true toll is likely much higher, as many people are still missing beneath the rubble.

sources.body: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) also called on legislators to tighten a law limiting the ability to prosecute sexual assault if a victim voluntarily became intoxicated.
sources.headline: Governor slams district attorney, Cornell police on handling of rape allegations

sources.body: About 20 states have laws that can make it difficult to prosecute sexual assault cases if accusers voluntarily drank or took drugs.
sources.headline: Cornell rape allegations reignite debate over laws on intoxication and consent

sources.body: RAPE LAW LOOPHOLE: Gov. Kathy Hochul vowed today to close a loophole embedded in state rape law around voluntary intoxification as she laced into Cornell University police and a local district attorney for their handling of a 2024 gang rape allegation. Under current law, proving sexual assault is difficult if a victim voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs. Individuals cannot consent “by reason of being mentally disabled or mentally incapacitated,” which generally applies to involuntary consumption of drugs or alcohol. Hochul said she would work with lawmakers “early” to change the law when they return to Albany in January. “Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape,” Hochul told reporters at her Midtown Manhattan office. “Period. I support closing this loophole and will work with the New York State Legislature to accomplish this.” The State Senate has consistently attempted to do just that through legislation , but the Assembly has yet to bring the bill up for a vote. Hochul also appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor on the case. Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff has agreed to an independent review. The plaintiff, a former Cornell student, alleged in a lawsuit that several men raped her at the Chi Phi house after coercing her into consuming drugs. The case attracted national attention after the student-run Cornell Daily Sun broke the story . The woman, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, told the Cornell campus police that she was “100 percent confident that she had been raped,” according to a transcript of her conversation with investigators . But that part of her account, Hochul noted, was omitted from the materials Cornell police sent to Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who declined to pursue charges without interviewing the woman. “In what world would the police learn from the victim that she had been literally gang-raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?” she said. “In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?” Earlier this week, James expressed solidarity with Jane Doe on social media . When asked about her decision to affirm the allegation, she declined to comment. Rebecca Valli, a Cornell spokesperson, said the university agrees with the governor’s decision. “We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State’s rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case,” Valli said in a statement. Van Houten, the Tompkins County prosecutor, said in a statement today that “we were not provided the full picture by the university.” — Madina Touré MARK YOUR CALENDAR: Join POLITICO’s New York Outlook: Affordability, Industry & The Economy on Oct. 14 for live conversations about the business and policy decisions being made today — from City Hall to the State Capitol — that will shape the city’s economic future. The lineup includes New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, New York City Economic Development Corp. CEO Anthony Shorris, Partnership for NYC CEO Steven Fulop, Citizens Budget Commission President Andrew Rein, Charles H. Revson Foundation President Maria Torres-Springer, and more. Register now to attend in person or watch the livestream . From the Capitol SPACE JAM: The fledgling United States Space Force is trying to find a home for its academy. State Sen. James Skoufis wants to make it so in the Hudson Valley, proposing that the recently formed military branch select Stewart International Airport. “New York Stewart International Airport would be an exceptional site for this project. It offers existing aerospace infrastructure — including one of the few runways in the country designated for space shuttle landings — alongside significant on-site development opportunities,” Skoufis wrote in a letter to Hochul this week. The Democratic state lawmaker is seizing on a NASA-led effort seeking input from governors interested in hosting or sponsoring the academy in their state. Skoufis wants to build interest in having the academy placed in New York, where some officials are trying to encourage growth in the space sector. “We built the Apollo lunar landers and refined the optics for every major NASA telescope,” said Patrick Chase, co-founder of Empire Space, a non-profit promoting economic opportunities in space. “The Empire State is the best location for the United States Space Academy, continuing our bold legacy as a pioneer of the American Space Age." — Nick Reisman BLAKEMAN’S VAGUE VOWS: Republican Bruce Blakeman has spent this year’s gubernatorial campaign focused on attacks — leaving serious questions about what he’d actually do if elected governor. With a month to go until Election Day, the Nassau County executive doesn’t have a policy section on his website. On the campaign trail, he’s opted against making detailed policy prescriptions in favor of going after Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani. When asked in August about his plan to reign in housing costs — a top concern among New York voters — Blakeman pivoted immediately to ideology: “It’s not through socialism.” “That’s a failed system,” he said at the time. “Mamdani the Commie and Comrade Kathy, they have this completely backwards because wherever they’ve instituted socialism it’s been making people miserable.” Blakeman’s policy agenda has focused on two major issues — massive tax cuts and an immediate 50 percent reduction in utility bills on his first day in office. But neither plan has been backed up by accounting that might suggest they’re plausible. His campaign declined repeated requests to release a plan detailing the cuts needed for the tax breaks. “It strikes me as very back-of-the-envelope,” said E.J. McMahon, who helped author former Republican Gov. George Pataki’s tax cut proposal. “A damp, coffee-stained envelope.” George Marlin, a former Conservative Party mayoral nominee in New York City and ex-director of the Nassau Interim Finance Authority, took such criticism a step further, writing in a Times Union op-ed today that Blakeman’s record on Long Island suggests he is not “fiscally skilled enough to merit a promotion to the state’s top job.” “As county executive, Blakeman has done nothing to restrain spending,” Marlin wrote. “Despite his misleading campaign rhetoric, he has never cut a penny in county taxes.” Blakeman’s campaign did not respond to Marlin’s attacks. Read more from Bill Mahoney in POLITICO here .  TROOPER ONE’S SUIT: A federal judge this week dismissed one of the retaliation claims against ex-Gov. Andrew Cuomo in a lawsuit filed by a former member of his State Police security detail. U.S. District Court Judge LaShann DeArcy Hall determined that because the alleged retaliation occurred in February 2022 — after Cuomo resigned from office — it did not constitute acting “under color of state law.” The woman, known in court documents as Trooper 1, alleged in the lawsuit that Cuomo sexually harassed her and that his former top aides subsequently retaliated against her. The former governor has denied any wrongdoing. “We respectfully disagree with the Court's decision,” said Valdi Licul, Trooper 1’s lawyer. “Multiple federal and state agencies found that Cuomo sexually harassed Trooper 1 and other women. We don’t believe his resignation in response to his proven misconduct permitted him to further violate the law by threatening one of his victims. We intend to appeal as soon as we are able.” Azzopardi, Cuomo’s spokesperson, responded: “Despite what Trooper 1’s attorneys may think, New Yorkers aren’t stupid, they know Governor Cuomo never harassed nor retaliated against anyone and a simple review of the facts by the courts is why their case continues to crumble, the same way 5 DA’s review of those same ‘agency reviews’ found no there there and the two civil cases against him were ultimately dropped.” — Nick Reisman FROM CITY HALL FINAL FRONTIER FEAR: At least one of the artificial intelligence firms set to testify before the City Council is supportive of the lawmakers’ regulatory efforts. Council Speaker Julie Menin plans to convene the entire body Monday for a hearing where leading AI companies will testify and provide input on a legislative package that would put guardrails around the emerging technology. In a letter sent Thursday to Menin and her colleagues — and obtained by Playbook — an executive from OpenAI said the firm is broadly behind the Council’s push. “We appreciate the Council’s focus on frontier safety, including transparency, third-party assessments, reporting of critical incidents and protecting whistleblowers, consumer protection, election-related deepfakes, and other key safety areas,” wrote Chan Park, head of U.S. and Canada policy and partnerships for OpenAI. “We also strongly support the Council’s goal of strengthening the City’s readiness to prevent and respond to AI-related cyber threats and emergencies.” In his letter, Park noted the ways AI is contributing to advances in science and education, but acknowledged the concerns over frontier AI models raised by Menin and the company’s own executives as part of a broad unease over how rapidly the technology is advancing. Park did not get into the particulars of each Council bill, but he noted OpenAI is also supportive of a state regulatory framework known as the RAISE Act and has been providing Albany with input on tweaks to the legislation and the state’s cybersecurity efforts. “Our own safeguards are essential, but voluntary company commitments alone are not enough,” Park wrote. “Enforceable standards, independent scrutiny, and public accountability are necessary to ensure that increasingly capable AI is developed and used responsibly.” — Joe Anuta IN OTHER NEWS — FLUSHING’S FACELIFT: As plans for a new “town square” in Flushing move forward, residents have raised concerns about gentrification and displacement. ( Gothamist ) — FOSTER CARE: Foster care agencies in New York are facing an unprecedented crisis of rapidly rising insurance costs, and they want state Democrats to approve a relief bill. ( Times Union ) — HAMAS HELPERS: The NYPD helped catch two brothers from Louisiana allegedly involved in a Hamas fundraising scheme. ( New York Post ) Missed this morning’s New York Playbook? We forgive you. Read it here .

stories.headline: Republicans shift Senate resources from North Carolina to unexpectedly competitive Kansas

sources.body: Senate Republicans are suddenly rushing to save a Senate seat in Kansas. On Friday, the Senate Leadership Fund, Senate Republicans’ top super PAC, reserved over $8 million in ads starting this weekend to prop up GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, according to tracking firm AdImpact. The spending in a state where Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in 94 years comes amid a deteriorating national political environment for the GOP. The impact of spiking diesel and fertilizer prices driven by the war with Iran, coupled with President Donald Trump’s trade wars, have been acutely felt in the heartland. Private polling from both parties shows a deadlocked race between Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state Trump carried by 16 points in 2024. “It’s a perfect storm,” said one senior Senate GOP aide, granted anonymity to candidly discuss the race. “The president isn’t making it any better.” Lower Costs Now, a new Super PAC affiliated with former Vice President Kamala Harris’ Super PAC, dropped about $700,000 into the state Thursday night, and Democrats are considering more spending to bolster Hamilton. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has been including Kansas in private fundraising pitches to donors, according to two people familiar with the conversations. It’s a remarkable shift in a state that was not high on either party’s target list just a few months ago — and shows the ferocity of the headwinds Republicans face in the final month of the campaign. “I think we're on track to win, but I am comforted to know that the cavalry is coming,” said Danedri Herbert, chair of the Kansas Republican Party. Herbert said Hamilton’s particular appeal as a pastor who heads the largest United Methodist church in the country, located in suburban Kansas City, made him formidable. “I personally know people who attend or have attended that church in the past,” said Herbert. “The ones that I know are right-leaning, and so that's troublesome. That's trouble — just the sheer ability to reach some of those people who are just always our people. I was telling national groups early on, like, ‘you should pay attention here.’” Republicans say the warning signs have been visible in Kansas for months as the agriculture-heavy state got hammered by a series of economic blows, including increased input prices from Trump’s tariffs, high fuel prices as a result of the Iran war, his decision to increase foreign beef imports , and heavy-handed immigration enforcement . As diesel prices shot up just ahead of the peak harvest season, the situation started to deteriorate even more in Kansas, according to Republicans. Vice President JD Vance visited Olathe, Kansas, in mid-September to campaign with Marshall, a sign of the GOP’s growing worries. Days later, he took a shot at Hamilton during a speech in western Iowa for having “kind of a ‘gee whiz, I’m a nice pastor’ vibe,” but said he “tells his congregation not about the gospel of Jesus Christ, but that they need to repent for their white privilege while eating beef” — a reference to a frequent attack line on Hamilton about his past calls to decrease carbon emissions . Marshall recently criticized the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement, saying recent ICE operations in western Kansas should have coordinated with local law enforcement. A handful of recent public polls have shown a close race in recent weeks. Hamilton’s internal polling and a recent poll for the Democratic Attorneys General Association shared with POLITICO found him tied or up a few points against Marshall. Republicans’ numbers are no better: One Republican involved in the race said a recent private GOP poll had Marshall down within the margin of error and said Trump’s approval rating has been underwater since summer in the state; another person said a different GOP poll of Kansas found a tied Senate race. “I take it as a compliment that the Republicans are now going, ‘Oh my gosh, we didn't think we were going to have to put money into Kansas, and now we're going to pour millions of dollars in to try to save Roger Marshall,’” said Hamilton in an interview on The Conversation with Dasha Burns , published Friday. “And I don't think they're going to save him.” SLF’s Kansas ad buy came as they pulled back in North Carolina — the latest sign of a deteriorating national political environment. And the agriculture-heavy Midwest has been particularly impacted by Trump’s policies. Republicans are currently fighting to hold onto Senate, House and governor’s seats in red-leaning Iowa and Ohio, and even redder Nebraska and Kansas. Retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) said the repeated economic blows to the Midwest were contributing to a series of tighter than comfortable races, including the Kansas Senate race. “It’s the policies and the chaos,” Bacon said. “That’s why Trump’s numbers are low. Tariffs are not popular in the Midwest and they contribute to the cost of goods.” National Republicans played down those concerns for weeks, arguing Marshall was still holding strong in polling and dispelling the belief that a Democrat could actually win the state. But privately, top Senate GOP operatives and Republican senators have been deeply worried about worsening economic conditions across the Midwest, increasing the states where they need to play defense. "He's running scared,” one western Kansas Republican, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the race, said. “I don't know if they took Hamilton for granted, but people are tired of Marshall not doing anything.” Asked for comment for this story, a spokesperson for the Marshall campaign sent a link to a New York Post article that details a $1.2 million buy for an ad that alleges Hamilton failed to report a pedophile who volunteered at Hamilton’s church’s camp; Hamilton’s campaign has previously said the attacks are false. “Adam Hamilton is a pedophile protector who would vote with Democrats like Chuck Schumer. He will never be the U.S. Senator from Kansas,” said National Republican Senatorial Committee spokesperson Samantha Cantrell. The SLF ad launching Saturday accuses Hamilton of being “a two-faced extremist,” and accuses him of “founding a radical group promoting the idea that all white people are racist.” "Adam Hamilton is running a strong campaign that’s giving a voice to Kansas families, farmers, seniors, and everyone being crushed by Roger Marshall’s toxic agenda," Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spokesperson Monica Robinson said in a statement shared after publication. "Marshall is right to be terrified that he will lose his job in November." Hamilton spokesperson Tyson Brody referenced a New York Times report about Marshall, a former obstetrician, and his involvement in lawsuits against patients who didn’t pay past due bills as he dismissed the ad barrage on behalf of a “failing” incumbent. “With this new ad, Marshall is turning to these desperate lies and false attacks because Kansans have learned Roger Marshall had pregnant mothers arrested and jailed over small medical debts, and voted to block the release of the Epstein files,” he said. Democrats have also hammered Marshall over the amount of time his family spends in Florida, where they have a second home . Hamilton is considering a late-stage fundraising swing later this month that includes an event in Boston, according to a person familiar with the planning and granted anonymity to discuss it. Democrats are bullish about the state, but are facing a cash crunch across the map that could hinder their ability to spread money so far that it reaches Kansas. Senate Majority PAC was already “actively thinking” about whether to wade into the state, its president told POLITICO last week. Democrats are growing bullish about other Kansas races as well. Recent polling has also shown a relatively close race in the fight to replace term-limited Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly as well as for attorney general. And the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added Kansas’ 2nd District, which Trump carried by nearly 20 points in 2024, to its extended offensive targets list Friday. “It's momentum, and that's what we're seeing across the state,” said Chris Mann, the Democratic nominee for attorney general. A spokesperson for Ty Masterson, the Republican gubernatorial candidate, pointed POLITICO to a mid-September Emerson College poll which showed their candidate leading Holscher 51% to 44%. The same poll found Hamilton leading Marshall 45% to 43%.

sources.body: Leading Republicans are pulling back from the North Carolina Senate race, sending a clear message: What was a top-tier battleground at the start of the cycle is no longer worth the money. The foremost Senate GOP super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, is pausing its future spending in North Carolina and instead launching a seven-figure ad buy in deep-red Kansas, according to one person familiar with the move. The news was first reported by Semafor . The dramatic change in strategy — less than four weeks before the midterms — comes after SLF previously spent more than $30 million to boost GOP nominee Michael Whatley. It also comes as public polling has continued to show Whatley unable to close the gap against popular former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic candidate. Republicans are now deprioritizing a state that President Donald Trump carried in all three presidential runs, and that Democrats haven’t won in the Senate since 2008. “We are all clear-eyed about where North Carolina stands,” said one national GOP operative working on Senate races, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. SLF isn’t the only major GOP group shifting away from North Carolina as Republicans focus on other must-win seats and deep-red states, amid the Iran war, high fuel prices and other economic fallout of the war in Iran. Earlier Friday, the Koch-aligned Americans for Prosperity Action left North Carolina off its $22 million list of future spending across key Senate contests, as POLITICO reported . Another major Republican group focused specifically on boosting Whatley — Old North Action — removed $6.5 million in ad reservations from North Carolina’s Senate race last month. “Michael Whatley is a good man who took one for the team — but with states like Alaska, Kansas, and Texas requiring continued resource commitments, there is only so much,” said another national GOP operative working on midterm races. “Especially against a very popular former Governor in Roy Cooper.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee is currently running coordinated ad reservations with six of its battleground candidates. Whatley in North Carolina is not one of them, according to data from advertising tracking service AdImpact. NRSC regional press secretary Nick Puglia said in a statement that “Whatley will put North Carolina families first by cutting taxes and keeping criminals locked up.” Whatley for months has struggled to boost his name ID against the much better-known Cooper. Some recent public polls show Cooper leading Whatley by double-digit margins. Private polling has also hardly budged, despite the recent influx of spending, according to a person working on the race. Trump on Friday told reporters he was "worried" about Whatley, his handpicked candidate in the battleground race. "He's a great man, and I am worried about him. I hope he wins," Trump said. "He's a great man, he was a great leader for the whole Republican Party when I won, and he'd be a great senator." In a statement, Whatley spokesperson DJ Griffin said the team feels “confident we have the resources” to win in November. “Roy Cooper recently said about federal elections in North Carolina, ‘Democrats are often ahead until they are not,’” Griffin said. “Undecided Voters who break late decide the election in North Carolina and the majority of those Late-Breakers typically go Republican.” AFP Action and Old North Action did not immediately respond to a request for comment about North Carolina. SLF declined to comment. SLF’s decision came as a shock to some, but not all, North Carolina Republicans — mostly because Senate Majority Leader John Thune has been scheduled to be in North Carolina for an event with Whatley on Thursday night. Thune ended up joining the event virtually, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. For weeks, top Republicans acknowledged North Carolina may be slipping away. One Republican who attended a donor meeting with Senate Majority Leader John Thune and SLF during the Dallas convention told POLITICO that holding the state would be “tough .” “The map has shifted a little bit, and to be fair, we knew that was going to be a tough one from the beginning," said one GOP operative working on Senate races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the landscape. Democrats are not letting up, recognizing that the contest in the purple state could still be close. "A Democrat has not won statewide federal office here in nearly two decades, and North Carolina is a 50-50 state,” Cooper campaign manager Jeff Allen said in a statement. “We’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them, while Michael Whatley will continue to enrich himself at their expense,” Allen said. One North Carolina GOP strategist said that while Whatley has been a “fine” candidate, the current political climate coupled with Cooper’s long record in the state may be too much to overcome. And while Republicans have repeatedly hammered Cooper on crime, he still has strong favorability ratings from his time as governor. “He's really kind of hard to paint as a radical, 'cause, you know, he's like Aunt Martha. She's just been there forever. And so it's just very difficult to get any traction on that, because, you know, people say, 'well, Roy's okay,’” they said. When told that SLF was moving money from North Carolina to Kansas, the strategist responded: “$6.50 diesel fuel will kick your ass.”
sources.headline: Top GOP groups retreat from North Carolina Senate race as hopes fade

Por sorpresa. El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, subió el viernes a la tribuna del Congreso . El jefe del Ejecutivo pidió valentía a los diputados del PP y Junts, que junto a Vox ya habían anunciado que no respaldarían los dos decretos de vivienda. Les emplazó a cambiar el sentido de su voto. Hubo incluso un momento en el que les rogó atender las demandas de la ciudadanía. Pero, consciente de que no iba conseguir la convalidación de los dos textos. concluyó su intervención con una frase que sonó a que ha llegado el momento de adelantar elecciones: "La historia les juzgará antes de lo que creen y con más contundencia de la que imaginan" .

¿Va adelantar el presidente del Gobierno las elecciones? A primera hora del viernes desde La Moncloa respondían que la única preocupación de Sánchez era el pleno y seguir presionando a PP, Vox y Junts para conseguir una victoria imposible. Sin embargo, el runrún sobre un posible adelanto antes de que termine el año ya había empezado a circular. De hecho, era uno de los escenarios por el que ya estaban apostando varios dirigentes del PSOE y miembros del Gobierno: que el desahucio de Maricarmen, la movilización posterior en la calle para exigir una vivienda digna y la derrota parlamentaria era una ventana de oportunidad única , con el foco del debate político puesto en un asunto que a priori beneficia a la izquierda.

Con Ceuta en un segundo plano, sin grandes novedades en torno a las causas judiciales que salpican al PSOE y al propio Gobierno, y ante unos meses que se pueden tornar complicados por la escalada de precios a causa de la inflación, para los partidarios del adelanto electoral en Ferraz este es el momento . Además, según su lógica, Sánchez no va a tener una oportunidad mejor de aquí al próximo verano, fecha límite para convocar comicios, porque lo más seguro es que todo vaya a peor. "Hay que aprovechar esta movilización" , defienden.

La prerrogativa de disolver las cortes compete en exclusiva al presidente del Gobierno. Sánchez tiene en su mano elegir el momento que más le puede beneficiar para apretar el botón , de ahí las carcajadas audibles del pleno del Congreso cuando en su alocución pidió al resto de grupos que se olvidasen "por un minuto del cálculo político". Hasta ahora el jefe del Ejecutivo había defendido que su objetivo era agotar la legislatura e ir a las urnas en 2027. En La Moncloa tan solo se habían abierto a lo que se puede considerar un adelanto técnico, es decir, celebrar comicios unos meses antes, en febrero o marzo . De hecho, era el escenario que hasta esta semana parecía más plausible: presentar Presupuestos, sufrir una más que previsible derrota en el Congreso, hacer de las líneas principales del proyecto la base del programa electoral y tener la excusa para disolver las Cortes.

Ahora todo puede precipitarse. Si a primera hora en el entorno de Sánchez aseguraba que su preocupación era el pleno, que no era el momento de plantearse un adelanto, una vez celebrada la sesión y certificado el revés, fuentes próximas al presidente trasladaban que el jefe del Ejecutivo va a sopesar este fin de semana si efectivamente ha llegado el momento de abrir las urnas . "Lo que ha pasado en el hemiciclo es muy grave. Vamos a abrir un periodo de reflexión", ahondaban las mismas voces.

Pedro Sánchez, este viernes a su llegada al Congreso para votar los decretos de vivienda

“La historia les juzgará antes de lo que creen y con más contundencia de la que se imaginan”, advirtió ayer Pedro Sánchez tanto al PP como a Junts.

El presidente del Gobierno culminó así su inesperada intervención ante el pleno del Congreso, justo antes de que se votaran los decretos ley de vivienda a los que fió –con el impulso de la indignación social que provocó el desahucio de Maricarmen–, la recomposición de la mayoría de la investidura y del curso de la legislatura.

Pero la suerte ya estaba echada desde que la noche anterior la dirección de JxCat –en una cita telemática a la que no se conectó Carles Puigdemont, según dirigentes de la formación– decidió tumbar las iniciativas con la moratoria de los desahucios o la prórroga de los contratos de alquiler. Así que las palabras de Sánchez –“antes de lo que creen”– resonaron ayer en todo el hemiciclo como una premonición del adelanto de las elecciones que ya empezó a sopesar la víspera ante el golpe de Junts a la legislatura.

El jefe del Ejecutivo rechazó tajantemente la demanda de los posconvergentes de retirar los decretos antes de que naufragaran en el Congreso, y que el Consejo de Ministros aprobara de inmediato un nuevo texto con sus “medidas efectivas” para atajar la crisis de la vivienda. “Este Gobierno no va a dar un paso atrás. Ha llegado la hora de la verdad”, zanjó Sánchez.

Así que el primer decreto ley, el único aún con opciones de ser convalidado, quedó ayer derogado por la mayoría absoluta de 178 votos en contra del PP, Vox, UPN y Junts.

De nada sirvieron las apelaciones de última hora de la ministra de Vivienda, Isabel Rodríguez, para que Junts se desmarcara de la derecha española, con una abstención que habría salvado el decreto. También cayeron en saco roto los ruegos de Sánchez para que “se olviden del cálculo político, del argumentario de su partido, de las presiones que les llegan de arriba”, y demuestren “si su preocupación por el bienestar de los ciudadanos es mayor que su deseo de dañar a este Gobierno”.

El Congreso derogó los decretos y Sánchez regresó a la Moncloa para encajar la derrota y evaluar su siguiente paso. Durante toda la mañana, ante el certificado de defunción que Junts expidió de antemano a las iniciativas con las que el Gobierno pretendía responder a la indignación social de la calle, el jefe del Ejecutivo empezó ya a pulsar la opinión de ministros y dirigentes del PSOE ante una situación que, para muchos, aboca al adelanto electoral.

El vicepresidente primero del Gobierno, Carlos Cuerpo, participó ayer en el Foro La Toja, en Pontevedra. Pero el responsable económico del Ejecutivo precipitó su regreso a Madrid antes de lo previsto, y llegó corriendo al Congreso: no para votar –no es diputado–, sino para incorporarse a las consultas que estaba evacuando Sánchez.

En el Gobierno y la dirección del PSOE, así como en muchas federaciones socialistas, ven que la enorme indignación provocada por el desahucio de Maricarmen la semana pasada en Madrid, y las protestas sociales y acampadas en la Puerta del Sol y otras muchas plazas de toda España, despiertan una movilización en toda la izquierda como hacía años que no conseguían. Y consideran, por tanto, que se abre una oportunidad que no hay que dejar pasar.

stories.headline: Housing protests spread across Spain after Congress rejects emergency measures

sources.body:
Centenares de personas han pasado la madrugada del viernes acampadas en la madrileña Puerta del Sol y en la plaza de Catalunya de Barcelona como protesta por la crisis de la vivienda . Una iniciativa que dura ya 6 noches y se mantiene con más fuerza tras la decisión de Junts de no dar su voto en el Congreso a los dos decretos sobre vivienda que el Gobierno someterá el viernes a votación en el Congreso. Ya se conocen como el 'Decreto Maricarmen' , la octogenaria deshauciada de su casa en Madrid, donde podrá volver tras llegar a un acuerdo.

EL PERIÓDICO abre un hilo directo con las últimas noticias sobre la acampada en Sol, las protestas por los alquileres y el decreto de la vivienda.

Cientos de personas se movilizan este sábado en Madrid para reclamar una vivienda digna y apoyar la convocatoria de una huelga general. La protesta parte en cinco columnas desde distintos puntos del centro y confluirá en la Plaza de Cibeles, frente al Ayuntamiento.

La marcha forma parte de una veintena de movilizaciones previstas en distintas ciudades españolas y está convocada por organizaciones de inquilinos y colectivos por el derecho a la vivienda. Pese a la previsión de lluvia, los manifestantes recorren las calles con pancartas, paraguas y chubasqueros para exigir nuevas medidas que faciliten el acceso a un hogar y regulen el mercado residencial.

Paralelamente, se están celebrando marchas en València, Cádiz, Sevilla, Palma, Guadalajara, Girona, Zaragoza, San Sebastián, Vitoria, Pamplona, Huelva, Granada, Valladolid, A Coruña, Toledo, Vigo, Bilbao, Logroño y Murcia, además de una manifestación prevista entre Barcelona y Hospitalet de Llobregat.

Miles de personas se manifiestan este sábado en València en defensa del derecho a la vivienda. La marcha, convocada por varios colectivos, ha partido de la Porta de la Mar y terminará ante el Palau de Les Arts, donde se celebra un congreso de inversión inmobiliaria.

Los organizadores llaman además a preparar una huelga general en noviembre y muestran su rechazo al bloqueo en el Congreso de los decretos de vivienda. Bajo el lema “Por el derecho a la vivienda. Fuera especuladores y rentistas”, la protesta reclama medidas para garantizar el acceso a una vivienda digna.

El Govern catalán estima que la primera convocatoria del programa Compra Conjunta, la medida para que mayores de 40 años con dificultades de acceso a la vivienda compartan la propiedad de nuevos pisos con la Generalitat, podría servir para coadquirir unos 2.000 pisos.

Así lo han explicado fuentes del Departamento de Territorio, Vivienda y Transición Ecológica de la Generalitat sobre una medida que el presidente, Salvador Illa, anunció el martes en la intervención con la que dio inicio al debate de política general.

La línea, dotada de 100 millones en su primera convocatoria, se destinará a la compra de la mitad de una vivienda por parte de la Generalitat para que cada beneficiario solo tenga que pagar el resto.

Javier Calvo y Javier Ambrossi, conocidos como los Javis, han mostrado su apoyo a quienes participan en la acampada de la Puerta del Sol de Madrid, España, por el derecho a la vivienda, porque "ponen la piel y el cuerpo para que las cosas cambien", según dijo Calvo a EFE.

La acampada en Sol continúa tras una séptima noche marcada por la protesta a modo de marcha nocturna hasta Cibeles

España se prepara hoy, sábado 3 de octubre, para una nueva ola de protestas por la vivienda , con movilizaciones en Madrid y otras ciudades en medio de un clima de fuerte tensión política después de que el Congreso tumbara ayer los dos decretos de Vivienda impulsados por el Gobierno de Sánchez. En la capital, la manifestación ha comenzado a las 12:00 horas, con cuatro columnas que parten desde distintos puntos de la ciudad.

El resultado en contra de los dos decretos del Gobierno, que incluían medidas para frenar desahucios y proteger a los inquilinos, ha puesto en el punto de mira la posibilidad de una convocatoria de elecciones anticipadas. Según fuentes consultadas por EL MUNDO, el presidente esperará a las manifestaciones de este fin de semana para decidir sin convoca elecciones, informan Raúl Piña y Marta Belver.

Mientras tanto, ayer por la noche, los acampados que iniciaron hace unos días una protesta a modo de acampada en la Puerta del Sol de Madrid, iniciaron una marcha hacia Cibeles en una protesta nocturna organizada por la Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista.

Sandra, abogada de 30 años, acude a la manifestación con su hermano de 27 años. Ambos viven con sus padres : "La situación de la vivienda es una catástrofe en este país. Los jóvenes estamos en una situación muy compleja. Da igual que tengas un trabajo decente. Nos vemos obligados a vivir con nuestros padres porque no hay posibilidad de independizarse. Además tenemos la carga social que se nos impone de que no queremos formar una familia y tener hijos, que solo queremos salir y divertirnos. La verdad es que no es que no queramos es que es imposible".
